title: Case Study 11: Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV) (Article 25 — Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal))
legalTheme: Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV) • Article 25 & Genesis Test
factualMatrix: In a matter instituted before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction), the Petitioner—an aggrieved citizen/association affected by a recent Municipal Corporation / Panchayat Authority action—challenged the constitutionality and procedural validity of an impugned executive notification and show-cause order touching upon Article 25 (Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV)). The Petitioner contended that Core constitutional framework under Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV). Further, relying on the evolution of doctrine through Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Petitioner argued that the State failed to satisfy the strict constitutional threshold and acted with manifest arbitrariness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal) before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction) is maintainable in light of Article 25 and constitutional remedies?

2. How does the principle of Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV) (Genesis Test) apply to the impugned executive notification and show-cause order issued by the Municipal Corporation / Panchayat Authority?
3. What is the controlling effect of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) on the validity of the State/Respondent's action and what relief follows?
statutoryApplicability: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 25): Under the constitutional scheme governing Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV), a Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal) before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction) is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 25 or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV)): Core constitutional framework under Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV). Applying the core concept of 'Genesis Test', the impugned executive notification and show-cause order by the Municipal Corporation / Panchayat Authority must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by Article 25(1) opens with the qualifying words: "Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion."

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)) & RELIEF: Guided by Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 25 is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Further, Article 25(2)(a) specifically saves laws "regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice", keeping secular matters within legislative competence.

factualMatrix: A constitutional dispute arose before the Central Administrative Tribunal / High Court Service Bench after State Government Department enforced a directive affecting rights and duties under Article 25 (Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV)). While the Respondent invoked broad executive/legislative competence, the Petitioner produced documentary records establishing non-compliance with procedural safeguards. Counsel on both sides anchored their submissions on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) and the doctrinal meaning of Genesis Test, requiring a structured IRAC determination on maintainability and merits.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Service Challenge Petition before the Central Administrative Tribunal / High Court Service Bench is maintainable in light of Article 25 and constitutional remedies?

2. How does the principle of Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV) (Genesis Test) apply to the impugned executive notification and show-cause order issued by the State Government Department?
3. What is the controlling effect of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) on the validity of the State/Respondent's action and what relief follows?
statutoryApplicability: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 25): Under the constitutional scheme governing Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV), a Service Challenge Petition before the Central Administrative Tribunal / High Court Service Bench is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 25 or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV)): Core constitutional framework under Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV). Applying the core concept of 'Genesis Test', the impugned executive notification and show-cause order by the State Government Department must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by All three statements are correct. In Duryodhan Sahu (1998) and Dattaraj Nathuji Thaware (2005), the Court held that service matters cannot be agitated via PIL, and frivolous petitions brought for oblique motives must be penalized with exemplary costs.

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)) & RELIEF: Guided by Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 25 is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Further, Both statements are true. The bifurcation of magisterial functions—placing trial, remand, and evidence recording under Judicial Magistrates (subordinate to the High Court) and law-and-order functions under Executive Magistrates—directly fulfills Article 50.

comprehensionMCQs.question: A temple management trust bars the entry of individuals wearing shirts or trousers into the sanctum sanctorum, requiring traditional unstitched dhotis. Direct the casino to offer 20% free tickets to the public

title: Case Study 200: Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV) (Article 51A — Original Civil Suit / Declaratory Relief)
legalTheme: Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV) • Article 51A & Legal Aid
factualMatrix: During proceedings before the Civil Judge (Senior Division) / District Court, University / Statutory Licensing Board defended an impugned impugned legislative bill / ordinance provision enacted/issued in relation to Article 51A (Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV)). The Respondent maintained that public interest and administrative necessity justified the measure, whereas the Petitioner demonstrated that Core constitutional framework under Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV). The Bench was specifically called upon to reconcile the competing constitutional principles established in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) with the Bare Act mandate of Article 51A.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Original Civil Suit / Declaratory Relief before the Civil Judge (Senior Division) / District Court is maintainable in light of Article 51A and constitutional remedies?

2. How does the principle of Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV) (Legal Aid) apply to the impugned impugned legislative bill / ordinance provision issued by the University / Statutory Licensing Board?
3. What is the controlling effect of Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) on the validity of the State/Respondent's action and what relief follows?
statutoryApplicability: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 51A): Under the constitutional scheme governing Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV), a Original Civil Suit / Declaratory Relief before the Civil Judge (Senior Division) / District Court is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 51A or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV)): Core constitutional framework under Religion, Minorities, Writs & Directive Principles (Articles 25–32, Part IV). Applying the core concept of 'Legal Aid', the impugned impugned legislative bill / ordinance provision by the University / Statutory Licensing Board must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by Article 50 commands separation of the judiciary from the executive. Judicial Magistrates exercise judicial functions independently under the superintendence of the High Court; Executive Magistrates have zero supervisory authority over judicial trials or bail decisions.

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)) & RELIEF: Guided by Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 51A is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Further, In Sunil Batra (1980), Krishna Iyer J converted a prisoner's handwritten letter into a Habeas Corpus petition under Article 32, establishing that procedural rigidities will not prevent the Court from protecting prisoners from torture.

comprehensionMCQs.question: The District Magistrate (an IAS officer acting as an Executive Magistrate) issues a directive to the Chief Judicial Magistrate ordering him to deny bail to all suspects arrested in a political protest. options: Comply with the directive because the District Magistrate is the head of the district administration

Refuse to comply, because under Article 50 and the Criminal Procedure Code / BNSS, the judicial magistracy is completely independent of the executive and subordinate exclusively to the High Court and Sessions Judge
Forward the directive to the Union Home Ministry for advice
Resign from the judicial service immediately
comprehensionMCQs.explanation: Article 50 commands separation of the judiciary from the executive. Judicial Magistrates exercise judicial functions independently under the superintendence of the High Court; Executive Magistrates have zero supervisory authority over judicial trials or bail decisions.

comprehensionMCQs.question: A prisoner confined in Tihar Central Jail writes a rough letter on a scrap of paper addressed to a sitting Supreme Court Judge alleging that prison wardens are inflicting electric shocks and third-degree torture on an undertrial in solitary confinement. options: Reject the letter because it was not submitted on green legal ledger paper with required court fees and verification affidavit

Treat the letter as a writ petition under Article 32 in exercise of epistolary jurisdiction, issue notice to the prison superintendent, and appoint an advocate commissioner to visit the jail and record statements (Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration)
Forward the letter to the local police station for summary disposal
Direct the prisoner to file a regular suit for damages before the Civil Judge
comprehensionMCQs.explanation: In Sunil Batra (1980), Krishna Iyer J converted a prisoner's handwritten letter into a Habeas Corpus petition under Article 32, establishing that procedural rigidities will not prevent the Court from protecting prisoners from torture.
